utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to wish a good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, as well as to Mr. Scott, his colleagues, as well as everybody else assisting us. Mr. Scott, you have 59 minutes left. We can have the witness brought in. Ms. Nozica, will your witness be ready tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, the witness is ready for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I will now give the floor to Mr. Scott, who will continue his cross-examination,

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel, and all those in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to continue on from where we left off last evening. We were looking at the report concerning events at Sovici/Doljani in mid-April 1993. I'll come back in a moment to the packet document that we were looking at and the other two related documents that we looked at right at the end of the day. Let me come back to that in a moment. We spoke the other day about packet communications. These were wireless or electronic communications being prepared and transmitted. We talked about that. Can you confirm to the Judges, sir, when a packet communication is being prepared, this is a machine -- this is an electronic machine where the text is keyed in; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said - I don't know on what day of my testimony - that I really have no real knowledge of packet communications, and I think when I spoke to you, I said that packet communications were, for me, a modern system of e-mail communications, but I really have no better understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if we can take -- if we can follow, then, your e-mail example, you understand obviously that when someone sends an e-mail or even what we might call today a text message, it is something that is keyed in, that is, using a keyboard; the sender keys the text into whatever apparatus is being used; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you appeared to indicate yesterday afternoon, if I heard you correctly, that you believe there are differences in the text between the hard-copy document, which bears hand markings on it, which we looked at, and for the record those two documents are P 02052 and P 02056, and you saw or claim that there are differences between those two documents and the packet document version, which is P 09790; is that correct, sir? Do you base your position in part on an allegation that there are differences in the text of the document? Is that what I understand you to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to ask you to let me look at the document, because it is much easier for me to follow if I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could have the usher's assistance, please. We have the binders on the -- if we can look at -- sorry. If we can look at -- you want to have the three documents at hand, but perhaps we can do primarily with two. The so-called hard-copy document that has some hand markings on it is P 02052, the packet document in the first binder, and the packet document, which is P 09790.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, while we're doing that, because unfortunately our time is limited and we don't have time to go through that document word for word, I'm afraid, or at least unless the Chamber would see fit to give us both more time, but I'm going to next ask -- and I'm sorry, Mr. Usher, I'm going to complicate your life further. I'm going to ask the usher to please put on a document that I'll ask to be given an IC number on the ELMO, and there are work copies to be handed out in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, that's for the ELMO? And could these please be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, this document for which you want an IC number, was it part of the 65 ter list or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a document that's been prepared simply for courtroom presentation purposes as you'll see in a moment. If I can ask the copy be given to Defence counsel and the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, while that's being distributed, so we can -- not lose time: This is a document, sir, that's been prepared by speakers and writers of the Croatian language, comparing the handwriting -- excuse me, the document, which is P 02052 and P 02056, and the packet document, which is P 09790, and I -- because of the shortness of time, sir, I'm going to -- I put to you that there are absolutely no significant differences in the text of the two documents that have anything to do with the content or meaning of that document. And I'd like you to go down, looking through that as much as you can, but I can tell you we're only going to be able to spend a minute or two on that topic, but I put to you that a review of that document indicates that the differences are few and trivial. I put that to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall go in order. The differences are not small or trivial. Look at the heading of the text with the signature and the heading of the text that arrived by packet communications. You will see that they are different. Secondly, even more importantly, look at the number on this document, of which you say that you received it from a witness, and look at the number on the document that reads "the Main Staff." They are entirely two different numbers. In the text, if -- in the document with the signature, there is mention of the army, "armija," and the document that reads "the Main Staff," it says "AR.BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's simply an abbreviation for the same thing, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the same document and the same author, he doesn't need to change anything in that document, but he sends it in the authentic version. In my opinion, the first version is the one published in the newspaper. I apologise. I don't wish to enter into a dialogue. I think it is not right to say that I am making speculations. I'm referring to facts that are visible to everyone in this courtroom. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, but time is short. You have no personal knowledge of the preparation -- the actual preparation of this document. You weren't there when it was prepared; you have no knowledge of how it was prepared. I asked you specifically about these documents. These are not Xerox copies. Two people would have keyed these documents in, one, either a typewriter or word processor, which creates a hard-copy document, which is the first documents, and, secondly, typing -- keying the message into a packet machine. Both those documents require the sender -- the transmitter to key those messages in; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I don't wish to interrupt, but there is some confusion. My learned friend in his explanation says explicitly these are not Xerox copies, but that is not true. We only have Xerox copying. That's all we have. We only have photocopies. We don't have a single original, and, of course, this is confusing for the witness. Simply, it is not correct to say that. The Prosecutor may present his submission to the witness, and the witness can respond, but by his submission, he cannot use untruths by saying they are not copies. They are copies. Everything we have are copies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I accept that clarification. What I meant to say, and I will correct -- I'll say it differently: The Prosecution's position and the position that I put to the witness is -- is that it is not like putting the same document on a fax machine twice, the exact same document, sending the same image twice. Yes, these are copies -- each one of these -- the packet communication is a copy of some original document. The other so-called hard-copy document is a copy. I understand that, and I appreciate counsel's clarification. My point, and my point to the witness is, and I submit to the witness is: This is not a situation where the same document has simply been put on the fax -- the same document has twice been put on the same fax machine. That's not the way this works.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, I take you back to your comparison of the document. So you say it's a big difference to you where one person writes out the armija, Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the other person keying the message in uses an abbreviation for the same thing; is that your position? That's a significant difference to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the most important difference is the number that you see on the top, and an important fact which no one has raised so far, which I will, this document with the signature was written on the equipment used for packet communications. You can establish that easily when you see the "cusa" [phoen], et cetera. Therefore, this document with the signature was typed in the same way as packet communications, so it is strange for someone to write a document in one version when sending it by packet communications, using one number, and then to change the number and make certain changes in it. And the most importantly of all, Mr. Marko Rozic is not head of the Defence Department. He is chief of the Defence Department, and he told me that he never signed it. And the stamp you see on this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's normal procedure that an objection is put prior to the offending question being answered. Your Honour, in this situation, the witness, and I have understood before on numerous occasions, firstly, Mr. Scott, with the greatest respect, is trying to squeeze, for understandable reasons, a lot of information in the remaining time, and I would ask, as Judge Prandler always reminds us, that there should be a pause between the question and the answer, because on several times the unfortunate appearance is given that the witness is being cut off. In this particular instance, it's very clear that the witness is not being allowed to answer his question, and I would ask that -- the witness is giving relevant evidence directly to the proposition put by the Prosecution regarding the document, and it's only fair, now the question has been asked, that the witness be allowed to give his answer. After that answer is given, of course, follow-up questions can be put in the normal way, but I would ask that the witness be allowed, as a matter of fairness, to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor has asked questions to you. You've provided answers. Is there anything else you'd like to say that you didn't say, or do you wish to supplement your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not -- I do wish to add to my answer. Mr. Scott did not allow me. The key issue on the document with the signature is the stamp that applied to the HVO. Bear in mind the Staff of the HVO in Jablanica and the stamps used by the department, and when I was giving testimony in answer to a question by Ms. Nozica, I presented the stamps and the times when they were in use. So when this document was prepared, this stamp was no longer valid. And even more importantly, Mr. Marko Rozic, who is the sender of this document, was not head of the Defence Department but was chief of the Defence Department in accordance with all the acts and documents that I referred to in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to make the record -- in response to Mr. Khan and in response to other comments been made, no, exactly makes my point. This wasn't an answer to my question. We're dealing with the topic now of comparison of the text, and I was giving the witness specifically the opportunity to talk about the comparison of the text. It had nothing to do with telling us for the 15th time that he claims that Mr. Rozic said he didn't sign it. It has nothing to do with the text comparison; it also has nothing to do with the text comparison, talk about the stamp. So the witness is wasting time, my time, precious time, not responding to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question, sir, is this: And two things -- and I do have to note in passing, it's just too big a point not to pass, just few moments ago, sir, you said you didn't know anything about packet communications. You didn't how they were made, and then you go on to express the view you know how this document was input, and I put it to you, sir, that it's a striking contrast of positions just a few minutes apart. Now, sir, apart from the fact that someone abbreviated "ABiH," can you tell us any other significant difference in the text of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a consequence of - with the greatest of respect and however inadvertent - a lack of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, leave respect apart for the time being. What I want to know is whether the document is a forgery or not. The issue of respect is -- I am a million light-years away from respect. Now, we have a witness here, whether he can say if it's a forgery or not. The Prosecutor says it isn't a forged document. The witness says it's a forgery. That's all we want to know. The rest is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a waste of time, but as Mr. Karnavas always says, I'm making a record. It is completely inappropriate for counsel to make comments as asides and not put a question. Mr. Scott prefaced his question with a comment. This is impermissible, and, Your Honours, I will say that for the record. It is inappropriate. A question should be put to the witness, not a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're right. You're right. Let's continue. Mr. Scott, let's go back to our business. Please continue on this document if you believe this is necessary and useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apologies. If we can go forward, please, to the documents that we were looking at at the end of the day yesterday, and we may need the usher's assistance on this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like a number for the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I please have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document before us shall be given Exhibit IC 912. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually, if I can have the usher's assistance, hopefully we can make the point briefer by putting this on the ELMO so that information can be shown, what's on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, in the interest of time, I've prepared -- I've laid the communication stamp information of the three documents, and I'll give the numbers for the record in just a moment, next to each other, which is now being placed on the ELMO. The top box comes from P 02074, which is one of the documents we looked at yesterday evening; the second box is from P 09790, which is the packet communication that we've been talking about; and the last box is P 10795, the third of those documents that we were looking at last evening. Now, sir, if you look at the packet communication, you will agree with -- excuse me, at that information that's on the ELMO, you'll agree with me, won't you, that these are three incoming communications to the HVO Main Staff, given numbers 2247, 2248, and 2249, coming in at the times 1745, 2300, and 2345, so that the document P 09790 comes in and is given the correct numerical order assignment and comes in in the correct time sequence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the documents you showed me yesterday and that we looked at today, these come in the order of the time. The date is the 24th of April, 1993, and the times are in sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you'll also look, sir, at the operations officer -- duty officer who's entering this information we've talked about several times during the course of your testimony, would you not look at those signatures on each of the three, and don't those look to you to be three same signatures of the same person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't wish to -- an expert for handwriting. They don't look like the signatures of the same person, but they are similar. Because of certain lines and dots, they're similar, but I'm not a graphologist, so I can't give an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you have voiced an expert opinion -- you have voiced an opinion over the signature of Mr. Lavric, sir, so is it correct, sir, that on sometimes you do feel the ability to give an opinion on hand-written -- hand signature and on others, you don't? Strike that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not so. Again, you're trying to lead me into an area, that even though I'm on the eve of my 70s, my concentration is quite good, and with regard to Mr. Lavric, I conveyed his words. So, please, there's a big difference. What I said is one thing, and if I'm conveying what someone else said is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. I think that is, in fact, important. So in concerning the Lavric document, your evidence before this Chamber is not that you know that that is not Mr. Lavric's signature, but all you have is somebody else's claim that it's not his signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lavric told me that it was not his signature, and when I was shown this document in the courtroom, I said that to me it also looks as if it wasn't his signature, but I relied primarily on Mr. Lavric's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, perhaps, can we go next, please, to Exhibit P 00463 in the binder 1, P 00463. While the usher is finding that, sir, this is an excerpt of a document the Chamber has seen before. It is the log-book of incoming communications concerning the HVO Main Staff for a period of time including 1992 to 1993, and I would like you, sir, if you could turn to the entry -- the numbers are -- there's a continuing sequence of numbers down the left side, and if you can please go to the entry for 2248, and for those in the courtroom using the English version, it will be the top of page 3. 2248. Sir, I think if you'll look at -- if you'll look at 2248, you will see it is the -- it is the log-book entry recording the incoming -- this incoming communication on the 24th of April, 1993, at 2300 hours from the HVO in Jablanica, directed to the Defence Department, S. Bozic's personal attention, and that is the document -- that is the packet communication that we've been looking at, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and never for a moment did I deny in this courtroom that the document was received in the Main Staff. If you remember, when Ms. Alaburic asked me whether this applies to the Main Staff, I said that it applied to a part of the organisational unit within the Main Staff, so that never for a moment did I question the fact that it reached the Main Staff, and I think there was no need for me to give any other comments. But it's important to point out what I said at the beginning, and that is that I never received it and that it was never sent by Mr. Rozic. That is what is very important in this whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you'll note on the communications log, just in reference to the documents we were looking at a moment ago, that -- and, indeed, the communication 2247 is logged in immediately before and corresponds to the document we looked at, and communication 2249 is logged in in proper sequence after that communication; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am not denying that this reached the Main Staff, but I repeat that I never received the document and that it was never signed and sent by Mr. Rozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can turn, sir, to Exhibit P 03220, P 03220 in binder number 1. And you can also -- with the usher's assistance, if we can also have P 03216, which is close by, immediately at hand. Sir, as I understand it, this Exhibit P 03220 is another document which you claim to be false in some way, and let me just be very clear. So it's your -- it's not your testimony that you say this -- the document is false because you recognise Mr. Lavric's signature not to, in fact, be his signature, but that you base your position on this document on what Mr. Lavric has allegedly told you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to repeat myself. I said that my position is based on what Mr. Lavric told me. When he said that, he didn't show me that document, nor did I see that document. When I saw it in the courtroom and when it was shown to me by Madam Tomasegovic, I said that this signature does not look like Mr. Lavric's signature, so these are two quite different things. When Mr. Lavric spoke to me, he didn't show me the document because he didn't have it. He simply told me roughly what the contents of the document were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you will look at P 03216, once again, sir, we have another document, a very similar document, coming from a different folder in the Croatian State Archive. And if you can look at that signature, you're telling us -- on 3216, are you telling us that that signature is also false?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's false at all. I'm not saying it's a forgery. Don't put words into my mouth, Mr. Scott. I'm trying to be precise, and -- precisely because I'm a lawyer, so I want to behave as one. I didn't say it was forged or falsified. What I said was something that I repeated already twice. I don't want to say whether it is false or not. I see that the document is similar, that the two documents are similar, in fact. But you say they come from different sources, but I see that both of them have two small stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So just -- because, again, it may be, sir, that some weeks or months from now the topic may come up again, so I just want the record to be very clear on what your evidence is and what your evidence is not. Your position concerning P 03220, as you've expressed it in court, then, as I understand your testimony over the last few minutes, is based entirely upon what Mr. Lavric has told you, and you have no independent information to add to that, one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, what Mr. Lavric told me, and I hadn't seen the document then, and when I saw the document, I gave my own opinion and said I don't think that it was Mr. Lavric's signature. I don't want to be exclusive. I say "in my opinion." That is my personal feeling, and I have a dilemma whether it's the signature of Mr. Lavric or not, so I can't say "yes" or "no." I can't confirm or refute, but I doubt it, and I told you what Mr. Lalic told me on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can go on to another topic. You discussed previously your involvement with the Department of Defence Personnel Administration, sir, and, indeed, I think it's fair to say, and if you will agree with me, that that was one of the sections and functions of the Department of Defence that you were most actively involved with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just confirm that I was at the head of the civilian sector within the frameworks of which was the Personnel Administration too. It had its department, and I was head of my own sector, and within that sector there were certain organisational units, one of which was the Personnel Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go, sir, to Exhibit P 02783 in binder number 1, P 02783. Sir, this is a document dated the 15th of June, 1993, coming over the typed name, at least, and again, I don't want to spend time debating with you whether you recognise the signature or not, but at least over the typed name of Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, it's a request directed to or stating: "For Mr. Slobodan Bozic personally: Subject, request for promotion of Convicts Battalion members to a higher rank." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I remember that. That's one of the documents you showed me while you interviewed me as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, that is, in fact, the type of document that would come to you and come to the Personnel Administration for the purposes of dealing with things like appointments, promotions, et cetera; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that isn't correct. I couldn't appoint anyone or determine ranks. This document came to the Defence Department, and as far as I remember, I answered at the time that nothing was -- it wasn't acted upon, and now I repeat for the Trial Chamber, this document was not acted upon for the simple reason that in 1993, individual ranks could be assigned, and the first assignment of rank in the HVO took place sometime in May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you communicate back to Mr. Tuta and say that, Well, I have your request, but I'm not able to take the action that you requested at this time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't consider that to be necessary. I didn't feel I needed to communicate, and you have the transcript of our interview, and as far as I remember, I thought that it was an attempt to have the -- have a better position for these individuals when it came to their salaries, but nothing was done as far as rank is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, telling me during your interview that you didn't recall ever -- during the time that you were serving in your various functions in the Department of Defence, you did not recall any occasion where you had any disagreement with Mr. Petkovic or anything that Mr. Petkovic did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do apologise, but I just didn't understand your question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time that you were serving in your various functions in the Department of Defence, you told me you did not recall any occasion where you had any disagreement with Mr. Petkovic or anything that Mr. Petkovic did. Do you recall telling me that in your interview?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have two questions there. First of all, I never had a disagreement with Mr. Petkovic, and I confirm that here publicly before the Trial Chamber. Now, the fact that I did -- disagreed with him, well, I don't know what General Petkovic did in performing quite a different function than was mine, so you're bringing me into a position now whereby, by asking two questions, two separate questions that don't follow on from each other, you want me to answer, and I wanted to give you a broader answer, which I've just done. But, no, I never came into conflict with General Petkovic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to move ahead to the topic of certain events in Vares and Stupni Do in late October 1993. On that topic, sir, you told me in the previous interview that you did not receive any official information about events at Stupni Do on 23 October 1993. My question to you is: Did you receive any unofficial information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I did not receive any information, whether official or unofficial, but later on -- well, later on, after a certain amount of time had passed - I'm not quite sure how much - I did receive information that -- for certain events -- about certain events in Stupni Do, but nothing special that I should know about in view of the job that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look at that. If you can turn, please, to Exhibit P 06182 in the first binder. P 06182. While the usher is finding that, sir, for the record I'll state that this is a press release issued by UNPROFOR on the 27th of October, 1993, concerning events in Stupni Do. We only have time to touch on a few highlights. The opening paragraph says: "UNPROFOR troops succeeded in entering the Muslim village of Stupni Do on the afternoon of 26 October 1993 and have confirmed that a massacre has occurred there." In the third paragraph, it mentions all 52 houses in the village had been burned to the ground; at least -- the bodies of at least 15 persons had been found. In the fifth paragraph, it starts -- it says: "The UNPROFOR troops initiated attempts to reach Stupni Do almost immediately after the HVO attack began on 23 October." In the following paragraph, the UNPROFOR commander says: "Despite the valiant efforts of NordBat, the HVO [Realtime transcript read in error, "UN"] troops systematically prevented the UN soldiers from entering the village of Stupni Do for three days." Over to the last paragraph in the document: "The investigation into the massacre and the collection of further evidence regarding war crimes will continue." Now, sir, since you've told us several times that you were the liaison officer with international organisations, including UNPROFOR, I take it, sir, that you saw this press release around the time that it was issued on 27 October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. I believe there is a mistake in the citation that you mentioned. You said: "In the following paragraph, the UNPROFOR commander says ..." And then the quotation: "Despite the valiant efforts of NordBat, the UN troops systematically prevented the soldiers from entering the village of Stupni Do for three days." I believe that not the UN troops prevented the soldiers, but they were prevented to enter the village by others, isn't it so, I mean by the -- I believe it was the HVO to which reference was made, and not to the UN troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Prandler, you're absolutely right, and the transcript should please be corrected. The document says: "... the HVO troops systematically prevented the UN soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I turn back to my question. You saw and were aware of this press release around the 27th of October, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me two questions before this one, so I don't know what to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Answer the question I just put to you just now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which question do you mean, do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you saw and were aware of this press release around the 27th of October, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to take care about what you asked me before that because you asked me about official and unofficial. This is a press release that any citizen could have heard about or read if it was published somewhere, and that has nothing to do with my function and post as a member of the Commission for Relations with UNPROFOR. This was a piece of information for the public because it says at the top here that it was a press release, therefore, a piece of information for the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question for the third or fourth time, sir. As the liaison officer with UNPROFOR, you were aware of this -- you reviewed and were aware of this document around the 27th of October, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this document as a liaison officer. I was aware of this press release as citizen Slobodan Bozic who heard about this in the press because UNPROFOR never put a press release of this kind to me, and we can see from the heading and title that it is a press release, therefore, for the public and for the press, for printing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me say something because it is up to the Judges to supervise this, and we have to avoid useless loss of time, and that enables us to interrupt occasionally and also do everything we can to be sure that the truth comes out. This is our role. We don't have much to do, but that is one of our essential roles. Now, the Prosecutor is asking you a very specific question. He's asking you whether you were aware whether this press release was given to you, and your answer is inadequate. We understood that you were the liaison officer with UNPROFOR at the time, and I imagine that this is an assumption that when UNPROFOR discovered what happened and releases a press release, and this is rather unfortunate, in fact, for the two women who were raped, they should not have done that, but these are soldiers, so we can't ask them to be aware of every aspect, but I suppose that when they have knowledge of this type of thing, they must come to you and say, Are you aware of what happened? I mean, that's the very least they can do. Otherwise, what is your purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that question, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, and this question gives me the possibility of telling you what my role was in answering. Now, on the territory, that was Herzegovina, conditionally speaking, and cooperation with those UNPROFOR units stationed in the area - they were the Spanish, then the British, and then the French afterwards - this press release came from the UNPROFOR headquarters, and you can see that if you look at page 2, the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb, and that is how this press release came to be made for the public. Had it been sent through the lower UNPROFOR units stationed in Herzegovina and forwarded to me, then I would certainly have acted upon this information. So that's how I wish to explain my position. It doesn't mean that my position as member of the Commission for Cooperating with UNPROFOR, liaising with UNPROFOR, means that I had links with all levels of UNPROFOR units stationed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To summarise, well, this press release came from Zagreb, and you are right, the spokesman from Zagreb was one to issue it, so you don't have any knowledge of it. But the second part of my question, which is the people at UNPROFOR, well, did they ask you for your opinion on what happened, or did nobody ask you anything at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. Nobody asked me anything with respect to this press release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as I take it, just to clarify again before we move forward: What you've said about this document is you were aware of it in your individual capacity, but it didn't come to you -- across your desk, you say, officially?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, there might be a problem with the translation, but the witness I don't believe said that he did have any knowledge of it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, did you have any knowledge of the press release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I heard about the document that was published in the media, not that I had received it. So Judge Antonetti, that was my answer. You understood it precisely, and you're quite right in what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my microphone does not [microphone not activated] -- Mr. Buntic [sic], you were asked did you have cognizance of this. You had. You had as a private person. That was your answer. You had not been served with it in your official capacity. That's another answer. But the answer was, did you know about it? You have said: I, as citizen Slobodan Bozic, had knowledge of this communique. Are you retracting this? Are you now saying something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that as a citizen, I took care that this document -- well, it's not a document. It's a press release. It is a release for the public, that the whole public in ex-Yugoslavia could have heard about and received this information. So officially or unofficially, I did not receive any information. The fact that as a citizen I came to learn of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Bozic, we must assume that you, as a lawyer, have a certain intelligence, and if that is so, then you should be aware when you're just repeating yourself instead of answering a question. Now, you have told us that the document could have -- everyone could have heard about it. That was not the question at all. It is obvious that if there is a press release, everybody could have heard about it. The question was: Did you personally take -- have knowledge of this? This is the question that you are repeatedly being asked, and you have to answer by yes or no finally. And, Mr. Khan, I think this is not -- you can comment afterwards. I want this answer. There has been so much time spent just for such a simple answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have a remark to make. Perhaps the witness can answer, but I do have a remark regarding Your Honour's insertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Make it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- recurring problem that we have. If I can take a number, I'm in the queue -- I was in the queue before Mr. Khan, and I'd just like to refer -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have asked a question, and I would like the witness to answer, and then I'll let you fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I want to say is this, that in the -- in translation, a document means something official, something that comes from a certain -- one organ to another organ, whereas a press release I see as something quite different. I knew or, rather, heard about this press release, and I take cognizance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are really trying our patience. We do not need lectures about what is a document or not, and you are not here to lecture the Chamber. You are here, and I quote myself, I said to tell us whether you have taken cognizance of this. I did not use the word "document." I'm sorry, perhaps I was too loud. The interpreters, please excuse me. I said that I had not even used the word "document" and that we did not need a lecture about the difference between a -- the interpretation does not seem to work. Is it all right now? Okay, I'm sorry. You still have no -- still no? Still no? This must be something for the technician. Can you -- I keep on talking now. It's embarrassing that it gets on the record, but it is merely to make a sound so that the accused can react whether they get an interpretation or not. So far ... I would ask the interpreters now and then to make some sound until this works again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll try something. Perhaps my colleague destroyed his microphone. Is it now working or not? Well, the best thing would be to have an early break, in that case. Let's have our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in session. The technical problems have been solved. Everything's fine. Mr. Prosecutor, you still have 24 minutes. Mr. Scott, after all these exchanges, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do appreciate that, but I do want to be clear. I don't know if Judge Trechsel has considered his question as still pending before the technical difficulties or if everyone wants to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. In fact, in fairness to the witness, I think I should give him a last opportunity to answer the question, and I'm sure he can remember because it was repeated so many times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I want to say that it is not my intention to avoid answering the question; far from it. And I said that as far as this press release is concerned, I heard about it from the media, not from any official sources, and I went on to explain this precisely in response to the question by Judge Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that case, this seems a very sensible point to make my submissions to the Trial Chamber before my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think Mr. Scott was before in line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I took the liberty of speaking to Mr. Scott on this issue on the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: He has nothing to say on this issue, so perhaps I may be permitted to make the submission that I intimated was relevant in this regard before he moves on either to a new topic or an unrelated matter. I believe that's correct, Mr. Scott; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to clarify -- that's true. I have no further comment -- in the interest of time, I have no further comment, of course, to reserve an appropriate response to what Mr. Khan might have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course. Your Honour, firstly, it is unfortunate that counsel has to stand up and make objections. They're not tactical devices. They're not simply for the joy of being heard, but there is a non-derogable duty for counsel that are acting for an accused to represent the client and appear as officers before the Court. I hope the intervention, firstly, is viewed in that regard. Your Honours, the transcript is before you. I'm not going to go through it ad nauseam, but in my respectful submission, whilst a number of questions were put on the same area, it does appear, with respect, that a lot of fuss is being made about very little. Your Honours will see in due course, at page 21, line 2 of the transcript, the witness referred to -- he made it very clear that if the press release was published somewhere. He has not said that he actually saw the press release. At page 21, line 11, again, he clarifies that point. Your Honours, page 22, line 24, to page 23, line 6, Judge Antonetti, the Presiding Judge, very properly, with the greatest of respect, put a question to clarify in a bid to get to the truth, and the witness was unequivocal in his response. Your Honours, there is a clear distinction, in my submission, between cross-examination and examination from the Bench. Your Honours, of course, there are sometimes long days. The witness has been in court and been in The Hague for a long period of time, and no doubt patience is wearing thin on all sides, and the Bench is only human, and no doubt on occasions all of us try the patience of the Bench; witnesses, counsel, and all parties. But, Your Honours, I'm sure that it would appear most unfortunate if an independent and impartial Judge, that Judge Trechsel is, would inadvertently, no doubt, give the appearance of being other than independent and impartial. Your Honours, there is always a jeopardy, borne of good sense and common understanding, why the Bench should be very loath to descend into the pit of litigation. Your Honours, the questions put by Judge Trechsel, for the record, in my submission, were unfortunately and no doubt inadvertently somewhat strident and somewhat accusatory. Your Honours, this is not necessary. It is not borne out by the scheme that the Judges -- the permanent Judges of this Court have crafted in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in which under Rule 90 there is

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: intervention of the Bench when they are seeking clarification, but I would ask that those questions be put with precision and carefully, but not with impatience or in a manner that it appears that the Bench is taking over the mantle of cross-examination from one of the parties, whoever it may be. Your Honours, I would ask that some care be taken, because it is important in a process to keep matters calm, that the accused are assured, as well as by standards of watching, that the process that Your Honours are struggling with, no doubt with all its difficulties, is fair, is detached, and is objective, and it's with that spirit that I do ask that Your Honour does take care in the mode of questioning. It must not appear to be cross-examination, which is the function of the parties. It should be questioning. And, Your Honours, I think that is something that is a concern of our clients. It's only important to -- one accused is already absent from this court. Your Honours are live of the consequences of that, and it is important to have a fair trial, that the accused feel they are getting a fair trial. And, Your Honours, I would ask that the spirits behind my submissions is taken on board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would react with two observations, Mr. Khan. First, I'm not very happy of -- with the way that you have cited the transcript because you have cited line 11 of page 21 but not line 12 and 13, which I had referred to and where the witness is reported as having said, I quote: "I was aware of this press release as citizen Slobodan Bozic, who heard about this in the press ..." So that puts a bit of different light. And the second point is: While I admit that I may have been a little bit emotional, you also have to recognise that we have had a lot of non-responses to questioning in a row, and I think it is understandable that someone -- that sometimes, though one tries to keep patient, there comes a drop that for a short while lets the barrel spill over. That is what happened. But I fully agree, in principle, with what you are saying, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's most gracious of you. In relation to substance, I didn't want to take time, but now it's been raised. Your Honours will review in the due course the entire transcript, but it was very clear to me, at least, that the witness was seeking to draw a distinction between the existence of a press release and knowledge of the contents of that press release. I think that was the issue that His Honour the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, got out of the witness and clarified it. But, Your Honour, there are consequences, of course, of being a professional judge, and I do accept, as I said before, that sometimes one's patience is worn thin, but I don't accept, for the record, that the witness was non-responsive. I think in order to get to the truth, precision is needed with questions, and the witness -- it may have been frustrating. There is translation involved. There were, of course, translation difficulties that were referred to before the break. But, Your Honours, I think the witness did try to answer the questions. It's a matter for Your Honours, after hearing all the evidence, to decide upon the credibility of witness, but that, of course, is not a license to descend, in my submission, into the pit, as I describe it, the pit of litigation, because there are consequences to the appearance of fairness when Judges do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, I definitely will not enter into a discussion about this. I think that would really be improper, which does not necessarily mean that I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, I listened carefully to what you said, as always, and what you say is always interesting, and it's always with interest that I hear you. I do not agree with part of your arguments. This is a mixed proceedings, a common law/civil law proceedings. When you say that the Judge shouldn't be, as you said, going down into the arena of litigation, I don't fully agree because we are looking for the truth, and sometimes in order to find the truth, we have to ask questions, to look at documents, to hear statements of the witnesses, and in everybody's interests, in the interests of your own client, in the interests of truth, we have to ask questions and look for the truth. I'm speaking under the control of the witness, who was a judge once, and he knows exactly what I'm talking about. Whether in Croatia, in Serbia or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, presiding judges ask questions and they look for the truth. Here there was a problem, a problem related to a press release. The Prosecutor was cross-examining the witness. He was trying to find out about the press release. The witness spoke. Maybe the Defence counsel have another viewpoint, and the Judges are trying to understand whether the witness had knowledge of the document -- of the content of the document, what he did at the time, and it is true, those questions, that we tried to seek the truth. Maybe we'll find the truth, maybe not. That's it. The issue of impartiality has nothing to do with it. If a Judge was partial, he would say the accused is guilty or is not guilty, but this is not what it is about. We're just looking at a document, and we're just trying to find out whether the witness knew about the document or not. It's nothing to do with the Judge being impartial or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with you completely. My principle objection was not about the right of the Bench to ask questions. I accept on many occasions it's most illuminatory, and it sheds an awful lot of light for the Prosecution and for the Defence on questions that are opaque or not clarified, but I do maintain for the record my primary submission that it does behove the Bench to ask neutral questions rather than, no doubt wrongly, give the impression that they are cross-examining the witness in the manner that is on the side of one party or the other. There's no need to ask cross-examination in order to get to the truth. The truth can be arrived at particularly by the Bench by non-leading, neutral, and rather balanced questions. But when one talks about the intelligence of a witness, as Judge Trechsel did, and when one talks about the Bench losing patience, it is perhaps unnecessary and lends more heat to the debate than light, in my respectful submission. But Your Honours, of course, the questions of the Bench are always welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Still at 24 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Sir, if I could ask you to look at P 06335, P 06335, and at the end of binder number 1 -- toward the end of binder number 1. Sir, you said you were hearing about these things in the press, and we've now heard over the last hour, including the break, about what you heard as a citizen and what was in the press, and I'd just like this one particular document - the Chamber has seen others; the courtroom has seen others - but this is an article from the "Times of London," 1 November 1993, concerning the events in Stupni Do. And again, sir, as a senior official in the HVO and as the liaison officer with UNPROFOR -- or to UNPROFOR, you were aware at the time, weren't you, that whether it was this article or other articles or CNN or BBC or Croatian Television, you were aware that what had happened in Stupni Do was a huge controversial issue at that time by the 23rd, 24th, 25th of October, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, it was a controversial period, not only in Stupni Do but in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about any other area of Stupni Do -- about Bosnia. Stupni Do and what happened there on the 23rd and 24th of October was a worldwide controversial event reported in the press and which you said a few moments ago you heard about in the press; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. In fact, I just remembered, and you have it in the transcript, that I told you when we talked that I heard this from the media, and you can check the transcript of our conversation. Unfortunately, I don't know English --

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: If we can go next, please, to P 06303, P 06303, in binder 1. This is an ECMM report, sir, for the 31st of October, 1993. I'll direct the courtroom's attention to the second paragraph under the heading "Political." I'm sure you can find that in the Croatian version, as well, sir. It starts with the words: "HOM/HRC". "Head of mission, head of the regional centre, head of the coordinating centre, and the political advisor met Jadranko Prlic, president of the government, CRHB, and Slobodan Bozic (deputy minister of defence CHRB). The meeting was cordial with open and frank discussion with head of mission again issuing the European Community demarche. Prlic stated that Bosnia-Herzegovina would never exist as a state, but all other options were possible. With regard to Stupni Do, he stated that General Petkovic, Chief of Staff, (COS HVO) had removed all local commanders, and an investigation was underway." Now, sir, do you know which commanders had been removed in connection with the events in Stupni Do as of the date of this meeting on the 31st of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this report, I see that I was present at the meeting at Mr. Prlic's, and that is something I referred to in the previous days, that I arranged certain meetings with Mr. Prlic with representatives of the International Community, this one included, at which I was simply the organiser of the meeting. As for your second question, which commanders were dismissed, I don't know what Mr. Prlic had in mind when he was speaking, but one can see from the whole text that my name is mentioned only as someone who was present, who didn't take part in the discussions.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, as the deputy minister of defence and as the person with primary responsibility with liaison -- liaising with UNPROFOR and ECMM, you must have gone into this meeting on the 31st of October clearly knowing, clearly knowing that Stupni Do would be on the agenda. Now, when Mr. Prlic said General Petkovic has removed all local commanders and an investigation was underway, I ask you again, do you know what commanders were removed? And that's my question. What commanders were removed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered clearly that I don't know what Mr. Prlic had in mind. And when you say that it was known, what the topic would be -- allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: You've answered my question, sir. You said you didn't know. That answers my question. My second question is, if you can assist us, if you don't know exactly which commanders were removed, do you know on whose orders or directions, whoever it was that had allegedly been removed, on whose orders were they removed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say, but I wish to tell the Trial Chamber that you did not allow me to answer your previous question fully.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Please go on to Exhibit P 06328, P 06328, in the first binder, toward the end. Sir, this is a document dated 1 November 1993 over the name of Bruno Stojic, recommending the conferral of the rank of colonel to Ivica Rajic of Kiseljak. Do you see that? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Would you please go on to Exhibit P 06339, also in the second binder -- excuse me, the first binder, it should be close by, P 06339. This, in fact, is a document -- it appears to be dated toward the bottom of the page, again, the 1st of November, 1993, by Boban, conferring the rank of active colonel on Ivica Rajic from Kiseljak. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Now, in reference to this event, this appointment of Mr. -- or promotion of Mr. Rajic to the rank of colonel, the previous document, the recommendation of Mr. Stojic, which is P 06328, as Mr. Stojic's deputy and someone that worked with him very closely, shared a secretary, had the office next to him, did you raise with Mr. Stojic that the promotion that Ivica Rajic to colonel on the 1st of November, 1993, given the controversies about Stupni Do, might not be the best thing to do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. In fact, I didn't even know that such a proposal existed.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Is it your position that despite the fact that you were Mr. Stojic's deputy and supervised the Personnel Administration, you're suggesting that Mr. Stojic personally prepared and signed this document without the involvement of you and your section?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't wish to say that Mr. Stojic signed that document on his own. This proposal could have of come from anyone who was within the Personnel Administration, within that small group. In any event, I don't wish to say that this was done by Mr. Stojic, but someone upon his proposal.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: And it didn't occur to you around this time, and I put it again to you, sir, given the nature of this controversy, I put it to you, sir, it's inconceivable that there was not discussion in the immediate office of the minister of defence about Stupni Do, the people involved in it, and the international concerns that had been expressed; and, again, are you telling this Chamber that as of the end of -- as of late October 1993, in fact in connection with the meeting that you -- in part that you attended with Mr. Prlic, that you and Mr. Stojic and others were not discussing the topic of Stupni Do and Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what we spoke about Ivica Rajic. I remember very well that I told you that this was a man I never met, I never saw him, and I didn't know anything about him, except for certain information that came after this that I now see as a proposal. Therefore, the meeting at Mr. Prlic's was not announced; that is, the topic was not announced. It was a meeting upon the request of representatives of the International Community without any indication of the topic.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: That's not my question now. My question to you was: You worked in the immediate office of the minister of defence or the head of defence. You were close by to him. You've told us before you were close to a lot of the senior staff, and I put to you, sir, that you could not have been involved in that position at that time with this controversy swirling around and not have had discussions with Mr. Stojic. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that I didn't talk to Mr. Stojic, and I repeat before this Honourable Trial Chamber that I didn't know that such a proposal for a promotion existed.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P 07546.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a brief technical question. I've taken a look at the document - as everybody else - carefully, and I've noticed one thing. Mr. Stojic recommends to Mr. Boban that Mr. Rajic becomes colonel. This is Mr. Stojic's recommendation, but my question is the following: Looking at the document, I realised that there is, first of all, Office of the President, Cabinet Predstojnika [phoen], but the Department of Defence was not part of the immediate office of the president. So why does this document talk about the Office of the President or immediate Office of the President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, this is the Cabinet of the head that formally existed but in actual fact was not operational until the end of 1993 when the ministry was formed. So this is the Cabinet of the head, and it's addressed to the president of the Croatian Community, at the time, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So it's the body that we discussed when Madam Nozica was examining me as a witness that were not functioning but formally existed, and one of those bodies is the Cabinet of the Head, not of the president but of the head of the department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, we read "Office of the President." Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another assumption. Please let me know if it's correct or completely incorrect. Looking at the document, in your language "Odjel Obrane" is "Defence Department." This was added to the letterhead. Would it be possible that Mr. Stojic went to the secretariat of Mr. Boban to make his recommendation, that the secretary took the usual letterhead indicating "immediate office of the president," that she added "Odjel Obrane" with her typewriter, and that she then typed in the text signed by Mr. Stojic? Would that be possible or completely impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, it is not possible, for the simple reason that these are two different positions. There's the head of department and the president. What referred to the cabinet of the head, it replies to the Department of Defence, and it is sent to the president of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna on behalf of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer, that sheds light on this document. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Sir, it's correct, isn't it, that the topic of Stupni Do remained on your screen, if you were [sic], and the screen of the -- in the minds, if I can put it that way. "Screen" perhaps doesn't translate well, but it remained on your minds and in the minds of the senior leadership of the HVO, not only at the end of October and November, but even into the following year, correct, 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Would you go, please, to Exhibit P 07546, binder number 2. P 07546. This is an ECMM report for the 10th of January, 1994. I'll refer it to you, and you can find it easily, sir, by its item number 2 in both the English translation and the Croatian language version, item number 2 under "A, Political Situation." And number 2 says: "The HRC and HCC met Jadranko Prlic and Slobodan Bozic, deputy minister of defence. Prlic was interested in ECMM knowledge of the alleged massacre in Krizancevo" - sorry for my pronunciation - "and HRC fully informed Bozic drew comparisons with UNPROFOR reaction in Stupni Do, which was immediate. HRC explained comparisons were superficial as an active confrontation line in Krizancevo prevented access at will and not armija conditions." So, sir, in this meeting in January 1994, for example, you were continuing to raise issues concerning or involving Stupni Do; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, at the time I was not deputy defence minister as is stated in this report. Secondly, this statement of mine, referring to comparisons with similar events in which the Croats were the victims, and as I said earlier on, I never wish to annul one crime with another; I'm just saying that one needs to have the same approach and same attitude towards every situation, regardless of who the perpetrators were and where it was done.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: I'd like you to go next, please, and I apologise for having the usher up and down, but in the interest of time, if we can move as quickly as possible -- my apologies and thanks. P 07352 in the third -- excuse me, second binder, P 07352. This is a document that the courtroom has seen before, dated the 27th of December, 1993, from Ivica Rajic to Milivoj Petkovic, and noting that the correct information regarding the new name is Viktor Andric. Do you see that, sir? Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Will you please go on to P 07394 in the second binder, P 07394.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm going to be giving another document or two, Mr. Usher, in quick succession, please. P 07394.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: This is an order from Tihomir Blaskic, dated the 30th of December, 1993, dismissing Ivica Rajic as commander of the Kiseljak Forward Command Post. Do you see that? Do you see it, sir? Sir, I don't have time for you to mark all the documents as you go through them. The record should show, just so the record is clear, that the witness has a highlighter and is marking the documents, which is fine, and I wish we had more time, but my question is, sir: Do you have the document? Apparently you do, and apparently you've now put a number of markings --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: If you look at the distribution or what's translated into English as "Submit to," do you see that General Blaskic's order dismissing Ivica Rajic, one copy goes to the HVO Main Staff and another copy goes to the Ministry of Defence, Mostar? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Would you please go next to Exhibit P 07401, P 07401. This is the order of General Blaskic, dated the same day, the 12th -- the 30th of December, 1993, appointing as the new commander of the Kiseljak Forward Command Post a man named Viktor Andric. Do you see that? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, but I've never seen this document before, nor the previous one.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: You'll see in the distribution, next to Mr. Blaskic's name, one copy, again, goes to the Main Staff, and one copy goes to the Ministry of Defence in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I repeat that I never saw this document or the previous one before.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Sir, based upon everything you've told us in the last some number of days about the workings of the DOD and the office of Personnel Administration, I put it to you, sir, that these documents could not have been created and were not created without them ultimately passing through your section of Personnel Administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying once again before this Honourable Trial Chamber that I never saw these documents and that I see them for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Sir, you told us under oath that during this time-period, and I was very specific about asking about the time and location, that during that time-period the Personnel Administration consisted of a total of perhaps five, six, or seven people working a short distance away from you on the same floor, and I put it to you again, sir: You were involved in and supervised your people in the preparation of these documents and documents related to it, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you are obviously neglecting a very important fact. Here, General Blaskic is dismissing and appointing and signing, and as far as I can recollect, he was the only military commander that Mr. Boban transferred such authority to. Therefore, this kind of dismissals and appointments have nothing to do with the Personnel Administration. Allow me --

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Sorry, no, we don't have time, sir. I'm sorry. I'm sure if counsel wants to pursue it, I'm sure she'll be given the opportunity. I specifically asked you, and you agreed with me, that on both of the Blaskic documents, they were sent -- both of them were copied to the Main Staff and to the Department of Defence. I submit to you, sir, that the reason they were sent to the Ministry of Defence is so they could be properly processed through Personnel Administration and be part of their appropriate file; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I never saw these documents before, and these documents were not issued by the Personnel Administration or prepared by it, but it was done by Mr. Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Then tell us, sir, who created the HVO personnel file for Viktor Andric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very easy to see that from the document that you've shown here. It was the Military District of Vitez. It has the number, the date, the time, and that has nothing to do with the Personnel Administration.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Sir, my question was not what was in Vitez. I'm talking about the personnel records that were kept by the people working under your immediate supervision. In the Department of Defence personnel file for this person, who created the Viktor Andric file?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by where this came from, someone did this in the Military District of Vitez, but I can't specify who, although we can see that it was signed by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, who in Mostar -- who in the Ministry of Defence in Mostar would have known to put any materials related to Viktor Andric in the Ivica Rajic file?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I seem to feel that this question presumes something which hasn't been discussed yet, and the presumption here is that somewhere, according to the Prosecutor, the Ministry of Defence, the Defence Department, there is a file which is called "Ivica Rajic" or I don't know what other name; that is to say, that they have a file on everyone. First of all, that should be the question, whether that is the case, and then, next, who created this file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, your time is almost over, so ask your last question. We'll have to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: If I can ask for my last question, sir, that you turn to Exhibit P 10783 in the second binder, P 10783. Sir, this is a document dated the 11th of July, 1995, from the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Ministry of Defence, Personnel Administration, over the name of Bruno Stojic, under the title: "Assistant Minister for Personnel." And this document is passing on certain information concerning Ivica Rajic. In the first paragraph -- in the first indented paragraph, Mr. Stojic does report that Mr. Stojic, on an earlier occasion, not in connection with Stupni Do, but on the 5th of March, 1993, Mr. Stojic dismissed Mr. Rajic. In the second -- in the next-to-last paragraph, above the name "Bruno Stojic," he does confirm Mr. Mate Boban has presented Mr. Ivica Rajic of Kiseljak with a decree dated 1 November 1993, which is consistent with the documents that the Court saw a few moments ago, granting him an active colonel's rank. Now, sir, is it correct that in this document prepared by -- over the name of Bruno Stojic, in July 1995, Mr. Stojic doesn't report anything about Mr. Rajic's involvement with Stupni Do, or the fact that he had been dismissed by Tihomir Blaskic, or the fact that someone named Viktor Andric had allegedly been put in his place? We don't get any of that information from reading this document, do we? Do we, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first time that I'm seeing this document, and what it says in the document I cannot comment on it. All I can say is that it is a text -- well, I can say what it says there. Whether -- why something was written or not written, that would be mere speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: THE PARTIES
utterances.text: You would agree, sir, that, for example, just in terms of the content, that it is consistent with the earlier documents that we saw by which Mr. Bruno Stojic recommended to Mate Boban, for example, that Mr. Rajic be promoted to the rank of active colonel? It fits with that document, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bozic, and thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, I have one question in relation to a question that was asked you earlier on. This will be very brief. Can we come back to folder number 1 and look at the log-book, P 463. These are the various telegrams that reached the Main Staff -- well, coming from the Main Staff or going to the Main Staff. Have you seen this? This is my first question. It's a very simple one. Were you aware of the fact that at the Main Staff, all telegrams were registered, recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I've already said earlier on, there was this one organisational unit in the Main Staff when there were these packet communications or telegrams, as you say, which were registered. I didn't know that a log-book was kept, but this confirms that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me ask you to look at the 9th of May, 2580 and the following ones. I will ask this question again when we have army people or General Praljak or Mr. Petkovic, but perhaps you could give us your opinion now. Looking at all these telegrams as of the 9th of May, if there was [indiscernible] from the HVO or the BiH, there must have been traces of that in these messages, and I see on the 9th of May that it starts at 3.00 in the morning, but it doesn't relate to Mostar. VP Mostar, which must be something that relates to Mostar, goes to Prozor at half past -- or at 2.55 p.m., but nothing else is said about the events in Mostar, apparently. Is that normal?
