What do you say about that? Whereas the 9th of May would seem to be an absolutely essential date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I said that I'm not a soldier and, therefore, can only present my own views or logical thinking, whether it will suit or not. Now, you heard why it didn't come from Mostar, because in Mostar there was the military district where the Main Staff was located, so they had the possibility of communicating in other ways. That's the only thing that I can say, thinking logically, but not as a professional opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answer. Ms. Nozica, I think you have follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to draw your attention that in the record, the response by this witness was not exactly transcribed. He said that in Mostar, both the Main Staff and the headquarters of the Military District were located, and, therefore, that information could be received or given out to either post, and that's not how it was recorded in the transcript. So could the witness just confirm whether that is a correct interpretation of what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that communication was possible between the Main Staff and the Military District in another way, too, in view of the fact that both the Main Staff and the Military District were in town and not too far away from one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's clear. Ms. Nozica, follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I ask the usher's assistance. Could he please hand out my documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I prepared for my cross-examination before the Prosecutor concluded his cross-examination, I'd like just to go back briefly to the last topic that was discussed by the Prosecutor and which he questioned Mr. Bozic about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, just to remind you, at one point when you were shown a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Starting from now, whatever you say will be taken off your time allocation. I'm sure you -- I want you to be clear on this. So time is precious.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am aware of that all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, when the Prosecutor showed you -- you needn't leaf through the document. For the moment, Mr. Bozic, I'm going to deal with some documents that were shown you most recently by the Prosecutor, but you don't have to take up the Prosecution binder. I'd like to ask you to rely on e-court, and I'm just going to show you two documents from the Prosecution binder, and then we'll move on to questions which relate to the documents that are in my own binder that you received today. Today, the Prosecutor showed you document P 7546, and that was a document dated the 10th of January, 1994. You don't have to look at it. I don't need it for my questions, and in that document, it says that you were the deputy minister of defence. Now, you said that in that particular document, that piece of information was incorrect. I'd now like to ask you to repeat to the Trial Chamber until when you were the deputy head of the Defence Department and when Bruno Stojic ceased to be the head of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that, but let me repeat. I was the deputy head of the Defence Department, while Mr. Stojic was the head of the department. To all intents and purposes, he didn't come to his office from the 10th of January, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: November 1993, correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and we were all relieved of our duties in the former HVO HZ-HB I think at around the 20th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I'd now like to ask you to take a look at the last document shown to you, and it will come up on e-court, and that is P 10783. It still hasn't come up on e-court. Here it comes. There, we have both versions. Now, this document is dated the 11th of July, 1995. My learned friend the Prosecutor asked you where this document was stored -- where the Viktor Andric document was stored. Can you confirm to the Trial Chamber whether we're talking about data referring to Ivica Rajic or Viktor Andric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without a doubt, it is information on Ivica, Ivo, Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is this a document of the Personnel Administration dated the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Personnel Administration from that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So obviously, the Personnel Administration at that time had a file on Ivica Rajic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, there were some documents for the Rajic file.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to ask you one more thing, and I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that Witness EA explained in this courtroom how the rank came about. I can't say more than that. Now, would you take a look at the information given. Now, there's paragraph 2, and does it say in paragraph 2 which post was taken up by Ivica Rajic on the 5th of March and that it was pursuant to Mr. Stojic's order that he was dismissed from that position? Is that what it says in para 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Now let's look at another document linked to information about Viktor Andric and shown to you by the Prosecutor. It is P 07401. Mr. Bozic, on the 30th of December, 1993, who was the minister of defence of the HR-HB, which post you held at the time in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of defence were Mr. Perica Lukic [as interpreted], and at the time I was president of the Office for UNPROFOR and International Organisations, and I said earlier on I did some work for personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, you have looked at a great many documents, both in the proofing sessions and the ones shown to you in the courtroom. Now, if a document were to be sent and addressed to the Personnel Administration, would it state precisely that, here where it says to whom sent, would it say if the document were addressed to the Personnel Administration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just for clarification, and apologies for interrupting counsel, on page 50, line 23, the name for the minister of defence at the end of 1993 was indicated as Lukic, and I believe it should be Jukic, J-u-k-i-c. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I've already learnt that corrections are made subsequently when it comes to names in the transcript, so that is why I did not intervene. Anyway, fine. We can now move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You were asked several times during your testimony here over the past six days where -- in what building was the Defence Department situated from the day that you started working there and onwards, and now I'm asking you very precisely. You said that sometime after the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO in May - and please correct me if I'm wrong - or towards the end of May, the Defence Department relocated from that location; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said roughly after the conflict, roughly at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did the Main Staff move out of the building too?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me where it relocated to, if you remember, and whether later on, after that period of time, when you, at the end of the summer and the beginning of autumn, as you said, returned, whether the Main Staff returned to that building too?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Main Staff stayed where it was. It was the -- a factory building.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript doesn't reflect that Mr. Bozic said in the building of a factory in Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, where did the Administration of the Military Police have its headquarters, if it had any, outside of this building? We're talking about the entire period -- well, you tell me what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police had a part of its headquarters in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was that throughout the period? I'm talking about the period from October 1992 until November 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be quite sure whether it was at the beginning of October 1992, but in any event the Military Police Administration had some offices in Ljubuski and others in the premises where the rest of us were housed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I have prepared two documents, which I think you have already commented on, so I don't need to go back to them, but would you look at the third document in your binder. It is document 2D 150.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we look at the number of employees in the Defence Department. Tell me, please, to the best of your recollection, the administrations and the offices and those employed in the offices of the Defence Department were added to this number? In other words, the employees in the Defence Department Administration and in the offices, are they included in this number?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I know this is an approximation - we never discuss numbers - but could you, please, tell us -- as this was one of the segments of your activities and which you supervised, could you tell us how many employees could have been in the administrations and offices, or if not, could you tell us, to the best of your recollection, how many administrations and offices there were at the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were four administrations, and then another five were added in Zepce, and within them there were offices. I don't dare give you the exact numbers, how many there were, but those offices existed at the level of the municipalities where municipal HVOs had been formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you can't give us an approximate number, whether this number of 247 figuring in this document, you can't tell us roughly how many employees there were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know which employees you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm referring to the employees in the administrations and offices of defence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, it depended from one municipality to another because in one report that we saw, the numbers of employees differed within the administrations or the defence offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. I won't insist on that. We will see later, if necessary. Mr. Bozic, let me move on to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, because time is precious: On that document about staff, within the Department of Defence there were 9 Muslims out of 247 people; is that a correct figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According to these figures, that is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 102nd and the 105th Brigades, in June, June 1993, because this document bears the date of June 1993, I can see that within those brigades the Muslims were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Your Honour Judge Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also see that in June, if I add up all the figures, that the HVO had 36.997, out of which 6.000 were Muslims, that is, one-sixth. Does that reflect the figures that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, because the document was obviously compiled on the basis of data available to the Personnel Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final question. The Convicts Battalion, and maybe we will talk again about this battalion in the future with all the witnesses still to come, I never noticed it before, but there are 280 people comprising this battalion. There are 164 Croats and 116 Muslims, which means that the Convicts Battalion is made up of Muslims -- that is, half of it is made up of Muslims, almost. Does that reflect what you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you asked about the 102nd and 105th Brigade. I just wish to point out that that will be the topic of the testimony of the next witness, so we will be able to discuss that with the next witness, so you have preempted my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... glad that we will be able to provide more detailed answers to this question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, let me now move on, in view of my own time and the Court's time, to cover a very important issue as quickly as possible, something discussed both by my colleagues, the Prosecutor, and the Judges; that is, the Defence Department. You have the Defence Department board. You have told us what that collegiate body dealt with and especially whether questions were reviewed at those meetings that had to do with the use of the armed forces. We will now cover all the collegiate bodies that we have. Unfortunately, we don't have more. But at the end, I will ask you what you know about the collegiate meetings that you attended and from which we do not have any minutes. I will briefly ask you to look at each of these meetings, and for the benefit of Their Honours, we will see which were the topics reviewed at those meetings. So let us look at 2D 1363. That is the next document. It is minutes from a meeting held on the 23rd of November, 1992; is that right? It is much more important, Mr. Bozic, for you to tell us what the six agenda items were.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are items relating to the organisation, the preparation of certain documents, certain current issues, personnel issues, more or less everything else that I would describe as administrative activities which the Defence Department was supposed to engage in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In this text, we have an indication of who was present. We have all the discussions, the conclusions. You attended this meeting. You did have occasion to see, during the proofings, that this is part of the subject matter reviewed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Look now at the next document, 2D 1443.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here we have three agenda items: a decision on salary rates, a decision on the acquisition of communications equipment for the Communications Department of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of HZ-HB, and current matters. Mr. Bozic, can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the topics that I described in answer to your previous question about the previous collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, can we look at the Document 2D 01444.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is minutes of the meeting of the collegium held on the 1st of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There are three agenda items?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I said before, topics relating to the administrative segment of the activities of the Defence Department, or administration profession, if you prefer to define it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, D 00880.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at all the agenda items carefully so that Their Honours, the Judges, can review them, too, should they have any questions to ask, so as not to be too hasty in your answers, what were the topics discussed? It's P 00880. Thank you, and I'm sorry, P.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All 13 agenda items, including current issues, had to do with administrative and professional activities which, in accordance with the decree, were entrusted to the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Look now at the minutes under P 01075.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm also looking at this document, and I'm wondering. You know we have a lot of questions, and we always try to look for answers to our questions. It seems that the Department of Defence, looking at this document, works with some kind of a collegium, of which members regularly meet with an agenda. It is presided over or chaired by Mr. Stojic. That's clear. And there are several topics that are being discussed, among others, the appointment of people. Now, when I look at this document with my glasses on my nose, I'm wondering, what was the margin of manoeuvre of Mr. Stojic in relation to that collegium? Was he completely dependant upon this group of people, and was he just implementing the decisions made by this collective organ? For instance, Judges, even when they disagree, they discuss matters and then they take a decision as a collective organ. As a Judge, I'm sure you know about that. In your opinion, first of all, since you took part in such meetings, do you think that the head of the department and then the minister of defence was the big boss? Was he making the decisions, or was he just implementing the decisions made by the collegium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. The last part of your question was not precisely interpreted for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll repeat the last part of my question. What I want to know is the following: As the head of the department or as the minister, was Mr. Stojic the big boss, was he the number 1, was he deciding about everything, as a leader would do, or in fact was he limited to the decisions actually made by this collective body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, at the beginning of my testimony I said that the collegium was an informal body which was not envisaged by any acts or documents, but the purpose of holding meetings of the collegium was that all topics of interest for the Defence Department and the preparation of documents and acts that were to be adopted at the level of the HVO HZ-HB or the president of the HZ-HB, should be discussed with the possibility of all members of the collegium taking part, the aim being to reach the best possible proposals and solutions that would then be further processed. Mr. Stojic was head of the Defence Department. He headed that department, but through this method of work all of us had the possibility of taking an active part, especially in the preparation of certain documents, as I just said, which were then further processed in accordance with the regulations of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I will ask you some follow-up questions after His Honour the Judge. If the collegium reviewed certain issues and took a decision, was this -- did this oblige all of those listed in the minutes? Did it mean that they had to implement it, even if -- look at this document P 00880, 880, item 9, please, if you can find it. I'm just giving you this as an example in connection with the question by His Honour Judge Antonetti. It says here that the decision of the HVO Mostar, dated the 13th of November, 1992, was reviewed, and it says that the collegium adopted the following conclusion: The mentioned decision is contrary to the decree on the take-over of JNA equipment within the territory of HZ-HB, and, therefore, it should be annulled, and the person who passed it should be informed as well as the HVO HZ-HB. If such a decision were to be adopted at the collegium, would that mean that such a conclusion of the collegium would be compulsory for everyone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And that was the case on a series of other issues, too, and listing these collegium meetings we can see that. Sometimes they made conclusions and certain individuals were tasked to do something; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. I think that brings us to document P 01075, and would you please -- well, I'm going to ask you something there, but take a look at the agenda and tell us whether they are the usual questions discussed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, let's focus on current issues, and then it says appointments to the Main Staff, and accommodation of the former Military Medical Clinic, and proposal of establishment ranks, and insignia of officials in the Defence Department. I wanted to discuss this topic with you at greater length, but I didn't have time during my examination-in-chief, but tell us, what ranks are these, establishment ranks, and what was discussed here? And we'll see this at the following collegium meetings, or maybe the previous ones; I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: I'm no military man, but as a lawyer working on these affairs, when we received information as to individual units from bottom to top and right up to the Main Staff level, then, along with the post performed by a person, without stating the name and surname, the establishment rank is set for that position; not for the individual, but for the position. So that is a forerunner to the future activities as to actually giving a rank. So this applies to the post, and that once somebody takes up that post, that post equals a certain rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. I would like to ask a question referring to the previous matter, where you said, Mr. Bozic, that the collegium took decisions that were binding for everyone. I wonder, what's the legal basis for this affirmation? Where is this set out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I said at the beginning that the collegium was an informal body, the formation of which was not regulated by any act or document, and in that way they wished to include all the close associates of Mr. Stojic to give them an opportunity to take part in the discussions and debates, to give their contribution as regards certain documents which would then go on through the regular procedure and through the regular bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly my problem. I do not see, really, how an informal body could take a decision that would be legally binding on everyone, including, I must suppose, Mr. Stojic. Is that really what you wanted to tell us? And if so, isn't there a problem about the legal basis for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the legal basis, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, you're quite right, because we're talking about the operative procedure here, and to all intents and purposes they wanted to arrive at the best possible solution or, rather, proposal for a certain act or document, which would then be passed through the regular procedure. So when you say that, you're absolutely right, that there is no provision that was in force at the time, but let me give you an example, the provision about assigning military apartments, for example. There were discussions at a number of collegiate meetings, and the ultimate proposal agreed upon by the collegium was one that Mr. Stojic, as head of the Defence Department, sent to the corresponding bodies of the HVO HZ-HB, and they were acted upon, and procedure was unleashed. So in this additional act, it does not say that this was the position of the collegium but that the Defence Department was going to act upon the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, you worked for a long time as a lawyer. Was that the only thing that you noticed which was not in conformity with what it said in the rules and regulations, this difference between the de jure and de facto? Was that a fairly frequent occurrence in the overall establishment of the HZ-HB? Can you tell us briefly something about that? And as we have very little time, then from the beginning of the establishment to these unfortunate events or, rather, the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've repeated this a number of times during my testimony over these six days, that it was a temporary organ of executive power, that we were not able to attend all the changes with rules and regulations, and I gave my example, that I was a member of the Commission for Relations with UNPROFOR and worked with other international organisations, as well, and very often the regulations weren't able to follow the de facto events on the ground which were imposed by the development of events generally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the final set of minutes that we have, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to this document, let's have a look at the current one, P 1075. I am a bit like Diogenes, who was walking in Athens with a lantern in daylight and he was asked what he was doing, and he answered, I'm looking for a human, a human being. I myself am looking for the truth. I'm the judicial counterpart of this famous person, and I'm looking for the truth. In this document, Mr. Akrap is mentioned, Zeljko Akrap. We've already talked about him. The collegium assigned him to the position of assistant within the Main Staff for training and education. Now, when I read this, I wondered what it meant. I suppose that the head of the Main Staff has plans in terms of education of soldiers and training. Why would an informal body impose somebody, that is, Mr. Akrap? We already know that he already had some responsibilities because an important document, according to you, was signed by him, so could you please explain to me how it all worked? How can an informal body impose to Mr. Petkovic, in this example, how can it impose Mr. Akrap as an assistant in charge of education and training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, we would have to read the whole of that part of the text, where it says the head, Mr. Stojic, informed the collegium that appointments are underway to the Main Staff, so this is just a piece of information for the benefit of the collegium, telling them that the Main Staff would be replenished with the various individuals. But no decision was made here, but it was just given as a piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I take note of what you just said. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I have a few more questions, ten minutes at the most. Somebody has just told me that it might be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like to have the break now? Remember, this is going to be the last break. All right, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would suit me, Your Honour, so that I could take a look at the document related to your last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it's convenient for you, very well. Let's have our break now, and you will go on with your redirect. After that, we will allow the witness to go, and then we will give the floor to Mr. Praljak and the other Defence for their part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Ms. Nozica, you have the floor. Therefore, the Praljak Defence to be able to do their part properly, you have only ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour, to wind up as soon as possible. But before I continue with the topic that I started discussing, I'd like to tell the Trial Chamber or draw their attention to the decision on the internal establishment of the Defence Department. P 02477 is the document number, and I'd like to look at point B. I don't have time to do that, but I'd just like to draw your attention to that because it concerned a question by Judge Antonetti, because it regulates how and who elects all the individuals to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, you spoke about that when we analysed this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, just briefly take a look at the minutes from the collegium, which is document P 04756, which is the next document in order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a meeting of the collegium of the 2nd of September, 1993, and take a look at the agenda there for the meeting, and these minutes are well known to us all.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as the previous one, that they were subjects which came within the Defence Department's remit as professional subjects to be dealt with by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My learned friend of the Prosecution asked you about the military prisons, and if we look at page 3 there, and Their Honours showed a great deal of interest for what it says there, so I'm going to ask you, Mr. Bozic, to read out what it says in these minutes, what Mr. Lucic said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I consider that we can't pass over the subject of the Dretelj prison and the situation there and that it can do us a lot of harm. We have to say exactly who stands behind those prisons, who is doing that, and what steps we can take in that respect."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we can read the rest in the minutes and the conclusions that were made. You testified about what was done pursuant to this request, so we can now move on to the next document, 4D 00575.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me ask you first, Mr. Bozic, whether you've ever seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we take note together that it is signed by Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And that it is addressed to the Supreme commander Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by the Prosecutor about the investigation into Ahmici. Would you read out the fourth paragraph of this document? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Ahmici case has been completed according to your instructions, and video footage has been forwarded to the chief of the VOS of the Main Staff, the HR-HB HVO-GS, Mr. Zarko Kesim [phoen]."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, did you know then or later that Mate Boban gave instructions to Mr. Blaskic to conduct an investigation or to do anything else with respect to the Ahmici case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. And I see this document for the first time, and from it I am able to learn those facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you to take a look at the last document in my binder, which is document P 7892. On page 2 of the Croatian text, we have the part that you were questioned about by my learned friend of the Prosecution, and it refers to the outbreak of the conflict between the HVO and the BH Army on the 24th of October, 1992, and that the minister of defence, Bruno Stojic, ordered that the team return to the area of Central Bosnia, and it says upon returning, the group submitted a report. I'm going to ask you first whether you've ever seen this report or a report of this kind by Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never saw a report, and I saw this report for the first time when shown by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, on e-court, that we have P 10028, the next document I'd like us to look at.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me stress straightaway that it is not my intention to tender this document, but I'm going to read out to you, Mr. Bozic, a part of that document, and it is the statement given before the Court by Mr. Petkovic in the Blaskic trial, and I'm going to refer to page 24177 of the transcript, and I'm going to read out what he says there. And as far as I know, Mr. Petkovic was answering a question from Mr. Scott, and I'm going to read the portion which relates to this particular report, and then I'll ask you a question. The question was this: "I would like to ask you to be provided with a Defence exhibit, Defence Exhibit D 250. It's in Zagreb. It's a report from the Vitezovi about their work during 1992 and 1993. Take a look at the second page of the Croatian version and the second paragraph there, and I'm going to read it out: "'After the outbreak of the conflict between the HVO and the BH Army on the 24th of October, 1992, the minister of defence, Bruno Stojic, the group returned an order telling them to return to the area of SB. Upon its return, the group tabled a report, and the number of the report is 1078/92, of the 24th of October, 1992.' "General, Bruno Stojic did issue orders, even for such large movements of units." And then it says: "There's an interruption. We've lost the connection. Have you heard my question?" And all we have is Mr. Petkovic's answer: "I'm going to give you an explanation. This was at the time when preparations were underway or, rather, when the operation called 'Bura' was underway in the Neretva River Valley, Storm, 'Bura,' and that was at the end of October and about the 11th of November, and first of all, I set the Vitezovi into motion from their deployment in Grude or, rather, in the area of Herzegovina. Similarly, I set other forces into motion from the OZ of Tomislavgrad which I considered they could set aside and join up for executing this operation. As far as I remember, the return of all the units to their previous positions I regulated with my order. I don't know what order of Bruno Stojic it was for them to return because I remember very well especially the units of the Tomislavgrad Military District and the rest, which were outside the OZ of Mostar, which I returned on the basis of my order. "Now, there is no mention here of the number of the order by Bruno Stojic. Therefore, I cannot claim that Stojic actually issued orders, and I claim that I personally ordered the units to depart and to return, those units who had taken part in Operation Bura." Now, the question is this: "Can you explain" --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have two short paragraphs, rather, three, to read out, and then I'll ask two questions, and that will be all. I'll finish with that, Your Honour:

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Can you explain how it was that Bruno Stojic, in addition to you, issued an order, or can't you do that?" "I cannot refer to Bruno Stojic's order because I haven't got the number of the order here. All I know is that on the basis of my own order, I moved the Vitezovi and the other units from the Military District of Tomislavgrad. I invited them to join the Bura operation." Now, my question linked to this document is as follows,

utterances.speaker: MR. BOZIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what the Bura operation was at the end of 1992, in the months that are stipulated here, "Bura" being "Tempest"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure, but I think it was during the war against the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, thank you. And now my last question: Mr. Bozic, did you ever hear - and you started saying something about this - whether -- or do you know whether -- whether the crimes were processed, crimes carried out against the Croats, in a place called Radesine, because you mentioned them, and Trusina, and Grabovica, and Doljani? What is your knowledge about that today, so many years after the events, after the crimes that were committed against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, unfortunately, there were no proceedings against any of the cases that took place either in Radesine or Trusina or Doljani. They were not processed, and as far as I learnt from the media, at Grabovica the direct perpetrators were taken to task but never the organisers or initiators, and my answer to your question is my own assessment and evaluation that I have already put forward when I spoke about the different relationship of individual representatives of the International Community towards the good guys and the bad guys, and unfortunately, what happened was this: I'm not going to call them crimes because it's up to the Court to decide whether it was a crime, but these criminal actions were never processed, and I'm even more worried and concerned about the fact that I know that The Hague investigators worked to establish and uncover all these incidents in the Konjic area, and I know that because I personally helped those individuals, and if need be I can mention their names, the names of The Hague investigators who worked -- who did their work, their research work, in the Konjic area dating back to that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, it would be very interesting to hear about your experiences. Unfortunately, my time has expired, so thank you for your answers during my redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic for Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Your Honours, that you will allow me to put some leading questions because things will proceed much more quickly if I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your name is Mr. Slobodan Bozic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sometime in December 2005, you made a statement to an investigator who was working for the Praljak Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have that paper in front of you. Will you please look at that document, especially the last page which you signed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had my signature verified with the notary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement, and do you abide by it as a whole, and is it entirely correct and complete in answer to the questions put to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I abide by my statement fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us state for the record the number of this statement, which Mr. Bozic handed in. It is 3D 03261, and it has been distributed to everyone in the courtroom. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness, and I will ask for this statement to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in accordance with Article 92 ter, you have asked a number of questions to the witness, and you have asked for the document to be put into the file. The other Defence counsel that have looked at this document, well, do they have any questions to raise in the form of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of General Petkovic is the first, according to our internal order. We have no questions for this witness in connection with this statement. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Coric has no questions either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we're going --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me end with the two others.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me ask my colleagues before giving you the floor, Mr. Scott. Let me ask my colleagues whether they have any questions to raise. No questions. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honours. Without giving any indication at all that we accept the evidence of this witness on this point or agreeing with any of it, which much of it we don't, we have no questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, thank you to all of the persons who took part in this. The Chamber will give its decision on this document after having discussed it among ourselves. Witness, I had some fears at the beginning of the week. These fears have now suddenly disappeared, and thanks to the speed of everyone concerned, this will allow you to go back home, back to your activities and country. And on behalf of my colleagues, I'd like to wish you a very pleasant return trip. I hope this will take place as pleasantly as possible, in spite of the storm, the rain and the wind. I'm sure this won't get in your way. And I wish you every success with your professional activities and duties. Let me ask the usher to take you out of the room now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wish you, too, success in your work, good health to everyone, and General Petkovic's early return, and I thank the Trial Chamber for making it possible for me to answer all questions as a witness of justice. Now, to what extent I was a credible witness is something that only you can decide. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica, now, for your witness tomorrow, unless he's already here, which would surprise me somewhat -- he isn't here, is he?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, it would really be too much of an effort if he hadn't already arrived. He is here and he will come into the courtroom, and I will be examining him tomorrow for two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have set aside two hours, the other Defence counsel have one hour, and Mr. Scott will have two hours too. Since we now have a few minutes left, we could take a look at the following week. There's no problem there. We will have the witnesses on time, will we, Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. As far as I can remember, next week we'll be working for three days. I think that is so. We have a break for one day. The witness will be here. He will be examined for three hours. That is what I assume. He hasn't come yet. I assume that everything will be in order. The direct will take about three hours, and for that reason I expect that we will be able to complete his testimony over those three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With Mr. Bandic, have you been able to consult with him, to talk about his schedule, because he had his -- well, Defence counsel for General Petkovic had expressed the need for Mr. Petkovic to be here when Mr. Bandic comes, so that automatically delayed things, so were you able to look at this issue of the forecasted schedule?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have been in contact with my colleague Ms. Alaburic. We have moved Mr. Bandic's testimony. As far as I can remember, we have postponed it to somewhere between the 15th and the 16th, but we are ready to make new schedules. We wish good health for Mr. Petkovic, that he may return as soon as possible. If he should return later than the date that we have planned, we will be informed about it. Mr. Petkovic's Defence counsel will inform us of this, and we will delay the witness until Mr. Petkovic is able to join us in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, we have had some good news about Mr. Petkovic, and through me the Chamber wishes to wish him a speedy recovery, and we will ask Ms. Alaburic to express those wishes. I would -- Mr. Prosecutor, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't want to interrupt the Chamber's agenda, and I was only rising that -- if it was at the end, that there was something I'd wanted to address briefly, but only if the Chamber -- only if you, Mr. President -- Thank you, Mr. President. I did want to use a couple of moments of time. Mr. Khan addressed the Chamber at some length this afternoon, and I did indicate at that time, I think correctly so, that I would not have any comments unless they were in response to Mr. Khan, and I'm now going to use only a small part of the time that Mr. Khan used in stating his concerns to the Chamber, and I just want to say this, that in certain respects --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Scott. First of all, I'm sorry to interrupt you. The Chamber wanted to express its wishes for prompt recovery to Mr. Petkovic first. Ms. Alaburic, would you like that to be done confidentially, and I will redact that, or is there no mystery about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I wish to thank you for your best wishes, which I will convey to General Petkovic. In view of the fact that we didn't enter into the details regarding his condition, I don't think there's any need for confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott, and so you want to react to what Mr. Khan said. I don't know what about. I certainly hope you're not going to light the fires of the issues again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do, as well, Your Honour, and I've taken that, believe it or not, into consideration because given the hour and probably the desire for those in the courtroom to perhaps be able to leave a bit early this evening. Nonetheless, and my comments will be short, I do disagree with some of the comments that Mr. Khan made, with great respect. I think it is the role of a judge to exercise control over witnesses, when a witness is unresponsive, when a witness is not assisting in the search for the truth. I think it's absolutely the correct role and function of a judge to intervene, and in fact, there have been several times this week in which both you, Mr. President, and Judge Trechsel have intervened when the witness -- when a witness has been unresponsive, when there has been wasted time by the witness, and I absolutely support both you, Mr. President, and you, Judge Trechsel. And if Judge Mindua were to do it and if Judge Prandler were to do it, my response would be the same. It is absolutely an appropriate -- in fact, it is one of the express functions of a judge to control the courtroom and to direct the witnesses when the witness is not behaving appropriately, and I think the interventions that both you made, Mr. President, and Judge Trechsel made were absolutely appropriate, and I thank you for it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do want to say something, Mr. President, in light of one of the words that was used by Mr. Scott. "The witness is acting inappropriately." I don't believe in any instance that this witness acted inappropriately. Well, that could -- I leave that up to you, Judge Prandler -- I mean Judge Trechsel. I mean, I do understand that there is a need to control. However, there's also the need to be perceived of being even-handed and to strike a particular balance at times, and I do think that when members of the Bench use a particular tone or use particular words, you know, in certain ways, it could give the wrong impression. As I understood Mr. Khan, I support his submissions in the sense that what he was trying to say, at least as I understood him, was we all need to strive to strike the appropriate balance, and when remarks are being made by members of the Bench to the witnesses, because the public is watching and because it may have a chilling effect particularly on Defence witnesses, it's -- we all need to be rather careful on how we phrase our remarks and the tone that we use. I don't think that it was meant in any way to disrespect, and I did notice, Judge Trechsel, that you shook your head. Obviously, you disbelieved the witness. Maybe you think he was trying to lie. Maybe you've discredited him already in your mind and you don't intend to give him any weight. I don't know. But it certainly says -- the behaviour that I saw, based on my saying I thought he acted -- he did not act inappropriately, gives one the perception, and it's all about perceptions, and we're not playing poker. This is -- you know, these gentlemen are here, and they watch everything, and they talk to us, and they put a great deal of pressure on us to react. And we don't react every time they perceive a particular slight or an injustice, but what I am trying to say, Judge Trechsel and Your Honours, is that perceptions do matter. And, you know, I'll be the first one to admit that my tone at times is inappropriate or that my word choice at times could be much better, but I don't think that when one of us stands up and makes a particular submission that it's done out of ill will. We're simply trying to convey our thoughts because our clients are extremely concerned, and I think that's all that was meant, and I don't think that the witness acted inappropriately. He may not have acted as responsively as some might think he should have. That's for them to decide. I don't know. A lot of things get lost in translation. A lot of these people -- this gentleman is still a suspect. He remains a suspect, so it could be that he's also trying to choose his words very carefully. Who knows? But, in any event, I do think that the submission made by Mr. Khan is one that is shared, at least by me, and I don't think that it was meant in any ill way. It was not meant to disrespect anyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, what I wanted to say was when you are a judge in this type of case, a very extended case, years and months are going by, it's very long, very exhausting, and we are overwhelmed by a mass of documents. You're well aware of that. You know that we have to take decisions about admissibility of documents. We look at each document in turn. You saw that in the decisions, sometimes Judges do agree, sometimes they don't agree between themselves, and that, of course, compels them to be very careful indeed when looking at the documents. So when you look at these documents with such attention, well, that means that the Judges have knowledge of the basis. We see witnesses coming in years -- up to 15 years after the events, and you know that sometimes you can't rely on people's memories. I, myself, am sometimes at a loss as to what I said in a meeting 3 years ago, let alone 15 years. And so what do we have? We have the witness's memory. And we have the documents. On the basis of the documents, we try to understand the scope, meaning of the document, to understand what the objective of the document was; and what we see, thanks to the help of the lawyers, is that we are faced with issues relating to translation. Yesterday, I called your -- the witness's and everybody's attention to the way in which certain words had been translated in B/C/S, and we have to be extremely wary of this, and I'd like to urge the lawyers who speak both languages to be very careful, and when they see that there is something wrong, to draw our attention to this because translation can sometimes have serious consequences. And I, myself, and my colleagues here try to uncover the truth by raising questions. Sometimes we're able to do that; sometimes not. In any case, we must not give in. Every time there is a document and a witness, we look at the document and we ask the questions that we believe are appropriate. We can make mistakes. Perhaps we ask questions sometimes that are not relevant. It's very difficult. You realise, of course, that we discover or look at these documents at the very last moment. As Ms. Nozica handed over her binder, there were a number of documents there that we had never seen before, and we have to, of course, react quickly, at which stage, of course, we take a close look at these documents. It could well be, and I agree with Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Scott, indeed, we are all under the pressure of time. Time is speeding by. Sometimes there is some ill temper. Myself, I sometimes am somewhat impatient because of the pressure of time, and we try to concentrate on important issues, and sometimes we simply don't understand why certain questions are raised, what their purpose is, and after 25 or 35 minutes, finally we end up by understanding; sometimes not, on the other hand. Perhaps that is one of the routes of some ill humour, but that's understandable. The trial is a very long one. We're overwhelmed by the number of documents. The implications are considerable, as you well know, and we also need your assistance, both the OTP and the Defence, to try to elucidate the truth. In any case, we make every effort, and we certainly hope that the climate will be better, that we are here to solve problems. We do solve some, perhaps not all, but we do our very best so that everyone can take the floor, that the counsel get the impression that the work they do is taken into account by the Judges, and that OTP also gets the impression that it is listened to, and who more than this Chamber has given to the OTP the same amount of time as Defence, so OTP has time for cross-examination. We try to listen to absolutely everybody. The best system, of course, would be for Judges to directly ask the accused questions. Now, the Regulations do not allow that. I, personally, am looking forward to Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic as witnesses. I'm preparing for that, and that's been going on for some time, and you will see at that stage that the questions will concentrate on what is essential, and I will do my very best so that what comes out is relevant. I, myself, and my colleagues make every effort to carefully listen to all parties and to take decisions when the time comes on the basis of as much information as possible. We could simply rest on our laurels and wait until people intervene, and then a few months from now there will be a judgement that will come out of the blue, as it were. We could do that, but that is not how I see justice, not international criminal justice. I think that Judges should ask questions as set out in the Rules of Procedure. We don't want to destroy cross-examination. Cross-examination does have value, but there can be neutral questions from the Judges, there can be ones that are complementary to the cross-examination or to direct questioning, or even after redirect, so that everyone is in a position to appreciate the scope of the questions raised by the Judges. Perhaps my colleagues would like to add something to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Almost immediately, I would have left it at that, but I think it might be misinterpreted if I did not answer the attacks waged against me by Mr. Karnavas, in particular. I thoroughly disagree with his appreciation of the way this witness responded, and I invite him to look at the transcript and critically examine how many times the witness did really answer the questions put by the Prosecution and how many times he simply did not. But I want to say something more constructive. I would really invite Defence teams to prepare their witnesses also for cross-examination and to tell them what we have heard so many times from Mr. Karnavas' mouth; namely, that unpleasant as it may be, that the cross-examiner, who may be Defence counsel or the Prosecution, has the right to ask questions that narrow down to a clear alternative, where the answer is yes; no; I don't know; I don't remember. It would really, I think, make the work of this Court much easier if witnesses would conform to that. I quite agree that there are cases where it is not really possible to say yes or no. I absolutely accept that. But basically as a rule, it is -- and as the Defence in cross-examination have insisted on this, I think it is correct that the Prosecution equally insists on exactly the same attitude by counsel, and sometimes - this has happened quite a number of times - when there is no response to the admonitions of the Prosecution, someone from the Bench will help out and recall that this is not a bad will of the Prosecution but that it is what the rules of the game ask. That's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no intention to attack you. You keep saying that I've waged attacks against you. I think making an observation is not an attack, nor is making a record an attack, and so if it was perceived in that fashion, I truly apologise. That wasn't the intention, certainly. I firmly believe that Judges are allowed and should be allowed to ask questions. I don't have a problem. I don't think Mr. Khan has a problem or anybody else. We did make an observation, but an observation doesn't turn out to be an attack. But, you know, as I've indicated, we are dealing in a courtroom where perceptions do matter, at least to some of us, and to our clients especially, and it behooves us to at least bring certain matters to everyone's attention so that we could have a fair trial, not just -- you know, both perception-wise, but also at the end of the day. But I certainly apologise if my observations seemed to be an attack. Normally -- I certainly didn't object earlier, and I certainly don't intend to -- my comments to be an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To follow up on the intervention of my colleague, who is absolutely right: When you speak to your clients -- to your witnesses, I mean, I think you need to explain to them how their testimony is going to happen. I think you have to explain to them that they are going to be cross-examined, that the Judges will ask questions that are different in form to the question asked by the Prosecutor, but that during the cross-examination the Prosecutor will develop his own thesis because he's looking for specific answers, and sometimes he will want a yes, a no, or I don't know. The Prosecutor through his questions is trying to develop his own case, his own theory, and you have to inform your witnesses about it. Of course, the witnesses you call are intellectuals. Many of them were ministers or high-ranking officials. These people are intelligent people, and it is obvious that for an intellectual to say just yes or no is always difficult because as an intellectual they always stand to explain a yes or a no or maybe to qualify their statements. You have to explain to them. You have to tell them that the Prosecutor will develop specific arguments. If they agree, they say yes; if they don't, they say no. And if the Prosecutor is looking for additional information, then he will ask follow-up questions, but you can trust the Judges, of course, and they will also ask follow-up questions, if need be. But you have to prepare your witnesses because it is exhausting for a witness to stay here for six sessions, four hours a day, twenty-five hours of questioning, non-stop questioning, that is. This is very tiring, of course. I'm convinced that the witness, when he leaves this Tribunal after a whole week, he's exhausted, intellectually, psychologically, because he's always listening to the questions that are put to him. He may be tense, and it's very tiring for him. That's why you have to try and minimise his stress as much as possible at the very beginning. I try to do so. I try to explain to the witness how things are going to unfold, but it's very difficult. If it was only 15 minutes or 20 minutes of questions, it would be okay, but it's more than that, and, also, there is the cross-examination, and the cross-examination is difficult for a witness. That's why you have to explain to your witnesses how things are going to happen because they have to know what they can expect. Well, I think you do. I think you do prepare your witnesses, but this is a recommendation from the Bench, and you have to explain even better because otherwise the Prosecutor will say, You haven't provided an answer to my question. Then you will jump on your feet and say -- and object to what's going on. It's better if the witness says no or something else, and then of course there can always be follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard that Mr. Praljak wanted to say something, but he let me speak first. I feel as if I have been called on to say something, as this is the case -- the Defence case for Mr. Stojic. I just wish to say that we absolutely do that with all the witnesses. We prepare them for everything that may happen in the courtroom, but we don't bring here abstract witness. We don't bring a concept of a witness. We bring here a human being who shows his reactions as a human being, and for me this is absolutely reasonable. We had similar witnesses during the Prosecution case; again, the reactions were similar to the cross-examination. But I have to observe that I notice a remark by His Honour Judge Trechsel which does concern me, and that is whether this witness answered directly or not, and I was concerned by this, as it was in the transcript. There's a certain opinion expressed by Judge Trechsel. But when talking about what you just mentioned, Judge Antonetti, we have to assess not only the way the witness answers but also the way in which the question is put to him. I am also a temperamental person, and if a simple question is put to me in a reasonable manner, even though it may be unpleasant, I will provide a simple answer. But if an individual is attacked by the question, then as a lawyer I have no right to expect him to be calm. So rest assured that we give our witnesses all the necessary information, but once they enter the courtroom, they are there in front of you, and it would be quite wrong to expect them to be puppets who have learned their lesson. They react in the way they feel they should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Since this a question of the Judges and the procedure had come up today and this evening, quite a very important question as it is, I would also like to add my own voice on that issue. Definitely, I do agree in general what both the Presiding Judge Judge Antonetti said this afternoon, I mean now when we are discussing this issue, and also in general what Judge Trechsel explained. I do feel that, of course, the Judges have a right to ask questions, as Judge Antonetti used to say, at any moment, according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, although myself, as you know, I would also prefer to have the questions mainly to be put, if necessary, at a later stage, mainly towards the end of the hearings and the audience in general. On the other hand, I also would like to say that I didn't find the remarks and position explained by Mr. Karnavas here as offensive against Judge Trechsel, although, of course, he may have criticised some of the positions and questions which were raised, but on the other hand I also would like to emphasise that the Judges' questions should not be, in a way, analysed as if they were one-sided. You have to believe us, that we are here for the administration of justice and with equal goodwill concerning -- and towards the parties concerned, and if we are asking questions, it is always led by the desire to establish the truth. And as Judge Antonetti also mentioned this afternoon, even if we, as we are humans, and everybody may make some mistake or a reference which could be misinterpreted, it shouldn't be taken as a kind of bad faith on behalf of the Judge or Judges concerned, but it is - again, I would like to emphasise - it is our good-faith duty to ask questions in order to establish the truth and in order to administer justice. So it is what I would like to underline, and although we know the saying that it is important not only to be fair but to look like to be fair, as well, also in this case I do admit that truth in that saying; but on the other hand, we should not always try to find in our questions and statements a kind of -- a bit of ill wish that would bring us against the interests of the accused. It is not our intention, not the intention of the Bench, and you may trust in our good intentions, as we trust in the good intentions of all the parties concerned here in this [indiscernible], as we used to say. So it is what I would like to explain, and I really feel that we shouldn't lose so much time with procedural questions. As you know, I am very much concerned about that, and I would like to have that the process is going to be led and going to be continued to the satisfaction of the parties concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak wanted the floor, I believe. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. Good afternoon to you other Judges. If you remember, a few months ago I asked something about some technical matters, the statements collected by my team, statements from the witnesses. My excellent Defence counsel, Kovacic and Nika, do give me answers, but sometimes I doubted -- well, I didn't know how and in what way the statements that took a lot of effort to collect, 180 statements, for example, and then this had to be repeated again because the Registry didn't want to give us certificates saying they were authentic statements. They say, Now, you in the Balkans have a right to go to a notary and so on to get them certified, and then we'll see. So we had to do this all over again, and as this requires a lot of time, money, and effort -- now, Judge Antonetti, I asked you during my -- well, the time for my Defence case is drawing near. Am I going to -- well, I counted 33 seconds to say good afternoon or good morning, this is you, is that your statement, goodbye. Many of the statements have already been translated. The Prosecution has staff members who understand Croatian. So I get good answers but not good final answers, and I don't know what's going to happen in actual fact. So even if we are talking about procedural law, and I'm not involving myself in that, I don't pretend to do so, but there's a lot of time lost on that, which means that not everything has been -- got through, so I wanted to ask that we don't get mixed up and entwined in witnesses and who has how much time and so on, that we could decide these matters in advance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, indeed, you've submitted the motions for the admissibility of certain statements. The Chamber, and I don't have the decision with me, but the Chamber has rejected the various statements that you wanted to be admitted into evidence. The Chamber decided in its decision that it was premature. We'd rather have your witnesses here, and those witnesses will cover the main elements of your arguments. Then you said that you would testify, so we'll hear your testimony, which will probably corroborate a certain number of issues, and then you will request the admission under 92 bis; maybe not of the 180 because that's a huge number - I don't know how many there are - but those which will come and complement the statements of your own witnesses or maybe of your own testimony. For the time being, we have 92 bis motions, but we don't really know in what kind of structure these statements will come and be tendered, so for the time being we decided that we would tell you this is a premature motion. We will wait until we hear your own witnesses, hoping that those witnesses will come and complement your own case, your own thesis. You said there were 180. I'm not entirely sure. I haven't checked the number. If there are 180, that would be a record because I don't think that in any case before, any party, whether the Prosecution or the Defence, has ever submitted 180 under 92 bis. It would be a world record, indeed. But if it's necessary for your own Defence, why not? Let's wait and see. Read the decision that we issued in which we explain what we want to do, and once we've heard your witnesses, once we've heard your testimony, maybe Mr. Kovacic and yourself will again ask for the admission of those 180, explaining that such statement is corroborating such and such an argument as it relates to such and such part of the indictment, and then we will review our decision. This is what I wanted to say to reassure you, but also to let you know that we are very attentive to this matter. On a personal note, I'd like to tell you, Mr. Praljak, but also talking to everybody else, the accused has the right to remain silent in these proceedings. Most of the time, you remain silent. In a two-month or three-month trial, silence, why not? But in a multi-year trial, I understand your position. Remain silent and sit back and wait, it must be for you very difficult, and I do understand sometimes you feel the need or the desire to take the floor and express your feelings, express a complaint. I do understand. I understand fully because in a criminal case the [indiscernible] is very difficult. The balance is very difficult. Everybody must have the feeling that he can be listened to. However, unfortunately, I didn't draft the Rules. I wasn't there when the Rules were drafted, but there is in the Rules a sacred principle, i.e., that the accused can remain silent and must remain silent. In other countries, in my country, for instance, when the accused is here, judges are allowed and free to ask questions to the accused. Here, another system was put in place, i.e., the accused must remain silent except when he testified as a witness. Of course, it means that you cannot take the floor freely, that you can only speak within the framework of the decision issued by the Trial Chamber. You've tried to quash that decision, but it was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber, and I can understand that you feel frustrated. It must be difficult for you to be there, to attend your trial, to hear the witnesses, to attend the cross-examinations, and to have to remain silent. That I fully understand, but that's the way it is, unfortunately. I hope you understand, too, it will get better after you've testified. We've used a D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6 system.
